Key Takeaways:

Three ambassadors presented credentials to President Ramchandra Paudel

India's Sudhakar Dalela was among the newly accredited envoys

Ambassadors from Laos and Panama also formally assumed their roles

Ceremony was held at the President's Office in Maharajgunj

Dalela is a resident ambassador, while the other two are non-resident envoys

Three newly appointed ambassadors, including India's new envoy Sudhakar Dalela, formally assumed their diplomatic responsibilities in Nepal after presenting their letters of credence to President Ramchandra Paudel at seperate special ceremonies in Kathmandu on Friday.

Related Articles India's newly appointed Ambassador Dalela arrives in Kathmandu Ambassadors' Club Nepal welcomes newly accredited diplomats

The other ambassadors accredited to Nepal were Vithaya Xayavong of the Lao People's Democratic Republic and Alonso Miguel of the Republic of Panama.

Dalela will serve as a resident ambassador based in Kathmandu, while the ambassadors of Laos and Panama have been accredited as non-resident envoys to Nepal.

title: Nepal's Balen Shah meets top Indian diplomat months after snub. What's changed? - India Today
description: Nepal's Balen Shah meets top Indian diplomat months after snub. What's changed?  India Today
publisher.title: India Today
full_article:
Around six months ago, Nepal Prime Minister Balen Shah refused to meet the Indian foreign secretary, which resulted in Vikram Misri's visit being postponed. Nepalese media reports then cited Shah's reluctance to meet with foreign officials who are not of an equivalent level. On Thursday, he sat down with the very same Indian diplomat. Perhaps, this time Shah's ego had to make way for pragmatism as Nepal just cannot brush away its largest trading partner.

advertisement ❮❯

Read Full Story

On Thursday, Shah met Misri in Kathmandu as the foreign secretary wrapped up his two-day visit to the Himalayan nation. It comes ahead of the Nepal PM's visit to India later this month (November 22 likely), in what will be his first bilateral trip since assuming office in March. The decision is another major turnaround by Shah, who previously decided not to make foreign visits in his first year in office. Balen Shah's visit to India later this month will be the first visit by a Nepal PM in three years (AP)Â

BALEN SHAH MEETS FOREIGN SECY

During his meeting with Misri, Shah was seen without his usual trademark sunglasses. Perhaps taking them off helped him see the importance of ties with India more clearly. The talks focused on water resources, energy, and trade, a joint statement said.

The U-turn is striking. Around six months ago, Misri had to unexpectedly call off his two-day visit to Kathmandu in May. While no reason was provided by India, a report in The Kathmandu Post cited Shah's self-imposed rule of avoiding one-on-one meetings with foreign diplomats.

The report, which quoted government officials, framed the approach as a "new protocol" where the PM won't meet officials below the foreign minister level.

It was not just Misri. Shah also refused meetings with US assistant secretary of state Paul Kapur and US envoy to India Sergio Gor earlier this year.

In the Indian context, Misri's visit was considered important to engage with the new leadership in Kathmandu after the violent Gen Z protests last year. Apart from trade and energy ties, Nepal's unique geographical position is key to India's security.

The snub to India came as the long-running border dispute over the Kalapani-Lipulekh junction resurfaced.

The tensions compounded after India and China agreed to reopen the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra via Uttarakhand's Lipulekh Pass. Kathmandu claims Lipulekh as part of its territory under the 1816 Sugauli Treaty. India rejected Nepal's position, describing its territorial claims as "untenable".

However, since then, Nepal has signalled that it was willing to address the issue diplomatically. In the background, engagements continued.

advertisement

In June, the chairperson of Balen Shah's Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), Rabi Lamichhane, received a high-profile and warm welcome in New Delhi. The next month, Shah broke his self-imposed protocol to meet Indian ambassador Naveen Srivastava.

WHAT'S BEHIND NEPAL PM'S TURNAROUND?

And then, flash floods struck Nepal. It left over 1,400 dead and 6,000 missing.

The flood, triggered by a glacial collapse in upstream Tibet, swept through parts of the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, swallowing towns, roads and bridges.

India acted swiftly to rush over hundreds of tonnes of emergency relief material and equipment like Bailey bridges to restore connectivity to far-flung areas. New Delhi also dispatched tunnelling experts and rescue teams to help workers stranded inside tunnels at hydropower projects.

According to the MEA, India rushed over 140 tonnes of relief material between August 26 and September 19, reinforcing its 'first responder' image whenever its neighbours face a crisis.

India also came in praise from Balen Shah in his first address at the UNGA in New York in September. In fact, the Nepalese PM also proposed a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism between Nepal, India and China to tackle climate-change-related disasters.

advertisement

The tone towards India had begun to change. Experts said there is also an important economic reason for Nepal to strengthen its ties with India.

Constantino Xavier, an expert on South Asian affairs, cited an economic angle behind the sudden shift in Nepal's approach.

"Nepal and other neighbours realise rising reliance on and benefits of closer economic relations with India to attain developmental objectives - especially given global slowdown and disruptions," Xavier, a visiting professor at Ashoka University, tweeted.

To buttress his point, he shared a news report from The Kathmandu Post that said Nepal has sought an economic package worth more than $2 billion (Rs 18,786 crore), comprising lines of credit and grants, from India.

The economic package came up for discussion during the meeting between Misri and Shah, the report said. A Nepal finance ministry official said an announcement is likely to be made during Shah's visit to India. There has been no statement from New Delhi.

Nepal said the funds would primarily be used to construct transmission lines and for reconstruction efforts following the flash floods.

THE GORKHA FACTOR

Crucially, Shah's move to pick India, and not China, for his first bilateral foreign visit indicates his eagerness to reshape ties with New Delhi.

advertisement

Another key irritant in India-Nepal ties has been the pause in the recruitment of Gorkha soldiers in the Indian Army following the Agnipath scheme. Under the scheme, introduced in 2022, only up to 25% of recruits would be retained for permanent service after four years.

This irked Nepal, which subsequently suspended the recruitment of Nepali youths in the Indian Army. It argued that the scheme was not in accordance with the 1947 tripartite agreement signed between India, Nepal and Britain.

However, earlier this week, India revamped the scheme to allow Agniveers undergoing training in the three services to join the forces as regular soldiers.

This is likely to create a more favourable environment for discussions on resuming the recruitment of Nepali Gorkhas. Coincidentally, the government move comes ahead of Balen Shah's visit.

For India, Nepal is a crucial piece in the regional security map. This is undeniable.

Five states - Bengal, Uttarakhand, UP, Bihar and Sikkim - share borders with Nepal. These are close to areas where Indian and Chinese interests overlap. Thus, for New Delhi, a Nepal that drifts too close to China will ring alarm bells.

For now, all eyes will be on Balen Shah's upcoming visit to New Delhi later this month. It will be the first visit by a Nepali PM in three years. The last visit happened in 2023, when then Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal travelled to New Delhi.

title: Nepali Gurkhas, Agnipath and a Himalayan Diplomatic Knot: Likely on Agenda During Balendra Shah’s Delhi Visit - TheWire.in
description: Nepali Gurkhas, Agnipath and a Himalayan Diplomatic Knot: Likely on Agenda During Balendra Shah’s Delhi Visit  TheWire.in
publisher.title: TheWire.in
full_article:
Chandigarh: The government's latest changes to the Agnipath scheme, extending Agniveers' four-year tour of duty by two more years, and offering them the option of permanent enrolment, could remove a major stumbling block to restoring the traditional intake of Nepali Gurkhas into the Indian Army.

Military sources said the resumption of Gurkha recruitment could feature in discussions during Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's official visit to New Delhi later this month, offering an opportunity to break the long-running deadlock that has soured ties between the two countries and halted the intake of Nepali recruits since the Agnipath policy was introduced in 2022.

Kathmandu has strongly – and consistently – opposed the four-year tenure prescribed for Agniveers and the prospect of 75% of these recruits being summarily demobilised with just a one-time, tax-free Seva Nidhi payment of around Rs 11.71 lakh, but no assurance of a regular military career or pension. Successive Nepalese governments had objected to what they regarded as India's ‘unilateral reneging’ on a major historic military agreement dating back to the immediate aftermath of Independence, without prior consultation with Kathmandu.

Shah is scheduled to arrive in Delhi on November 22 for a three-day stay, his first foreign trip since taking office in March and follows Indian foreign secretary Vikram Misri's November 4–5 visit to Kathmandu, during which the two sides discussed possible outcomes and initiatives across their bilateral relationship.

Official sources said restoring Gurkha recruitment could be a significant step towards repairing strained ties between Delhi and Kathmandu, particularly in light of the fact that Nepal was broadening its strategic and military engagement with China.

Demand to revivive the longstanding arrangement

The Gurkha recruitment freeze has, over the past four years, become a major irritant in an already troubled bilateral relationship, burdened by mutual mistrust over territorial disputes involving the Kalapani, Lipulekh and Limpiyadhura border regions alongside Delhi’s serious concerns over China's growing security, political and diplomatic engagement with Nepal. These strains were also evident in the postponement of Misri's planned May visit to Nepal amid differences over protocol and the border disputes.

There has also been enduring pressure from Nepal’s Gurkha veteran community to revive the longstanding arrangement under which Nepali youths could enlist in the Indian Army on the previously established terms, that include full-length service tenures and lifelong pension rights. During Indian Army Chief General Dhiraj Seth's visit to Nepal in August, Gurkha veterans had raised the recruitment freeze with him in Pokhara, a major recruitment centre in western Nepal, and urged him to lift the suspension.

Gaj Bahadur Thapa, vice-president of the Nepal Bharatiya Gorkha Sainik Board, made a specific appeal to General Seth at a gathering of veterans, but he declined to comment. Media reports of Gen Seth’s visit also made no mention of the issue featuring in his formal discussions with Prime Minister Shah, who also holds the defence portfolio, or Nepal’s Army Chief, Gen Ashok Raj Sigdel.

“Restoring the traditional intake of Nepali Gurkhas would carry significance well beyond the respective armies “ said a retired one-star Gurkha regiment officer in Chandigarh. "It could also help revive one of the oldest and most tangible institutional links between the two countries," he added, "declining to be named and the recent changes to the Agnipath scheme, could well help break this deadlock”.

The longstanding military association between the two countries is pegged to the Tripartite Agreement between Nepal, Britain and India, concluded by the Joint Partition Committee in November 1947, three months after India's independence.

Under this arrangement, the Indian Army routinely recruited over 1,400 Nepali Gurkhas annually. Before the recruitment freeze in 2022, 32,000–36,000 Nepali Gurkhas were serving in the Army's seven Gurkha regiments, making their presence a durable bond between the neighbours.

This relationship also has a significant economic dimension.

An estimated 1,25,000–1,35,000 former Indian Army Gurkhas, living in Nepal received annual pensions estimated at around $620 million — significantly more than Kathmandu's yearly defence expenditure of approximately $436 million in 2024–25. India's Military Pension Branch, headquartered in Kathmandu, channelled these payments through two Pension Paying Offices, at Pokhara and Dharan in the east and in recent years, via online banking channels.

Collectively, these pensions are a crucial financial lifeline for tens of thousands of Gurkha families in Nepal, keeping economies afloat in communities that have a long tradition of sending their sons to serve in the Indian Army. And while the pension flow continued uninterrupted after Gurkha intake into the Indian Army was suspended in 2022, the freeze cut off the pipeline of future Gurkha aspirants across large parts of Nepal's traditional recruiting heartlands.

The revised Agnipath arrangement announced on Wednesday by Chief of Defence Staff General N.S. Raja Subramani, following government approval, could to a large degree address many of Kathmandu's objections by allowing Nepali Gurkha Agniveers to serve for two years beyond the initial four-year tenure, and then pot for regular colour service.

“For Kathmandu, this would be a highly acceptable proposition from the original scheme,” said the retired Army officer quoted earlier. Whether the revised terms go far enough to satisfy Nepal will eventually emerge from discussions between the two governments and military establishments, he added.

An opportunity for India to resolve the impasse

Other Indian Army Gurkha regiment veterans advised caution.

They said Nepal would almost certainly want clarity on whether the revised arrangement met the provisions of the 1947 agreement relating to length of service, pensions and retirement benefits. “For now, it also remains unclear whether the extended six-year Agniveer tenure, by itself, would qualify a soldier for pension entitlements,” said a three-star officer.

Simply announcing an extension, without spelling out what it means for long-term service and retirement benefits, is unlikely to be enough to persuade Kathmandu to agree to the resumption of Gurkha recruitment, he cautioned, requesting anonymity.

Also read: Agniveers Can Marry, But if Killed No Pension to Family, Dependents: Report

Gurkha service in the Indian Army began under colonial rule in the early 19th century, when the British began recruiting soldiers from Nepal following the Anglo-Nepal War and the Treaty of Sugauli in 1816. The first Gurkha regiment had, in fact, been raised a year earlier, in 1815, by the British East India Company as the Nasiri Regiment, later renamed the 1st King George’s Own Gurkha Rifles.

The British Indian Army retained the Gurkha regiments until Independence, after which their future was settled under the 1947 agreement between India, Britain and Nepal referred to earlier. Of the ten regiments, six opted to remain with the Indian Army, while four — 2GR, 6GR, 7GR and 10GR — transferred to British service. India subsequently raised a seventh Gurkha regiment from among those who had declined transfer to the British Army.

Unlike the British Army, the Indian Army imposed no restrictions on Gurkhas becoming commissioned officers, and many eventually rose to senior command positions. A separate agreement also provided for Gurkha soldiers serving in both armies to receive equal pay and comparable pension benefits. These arrangements were revised in the early 2000s, after a prolonged campaign by the media and veterans' activists led the UK to substantially hike pensions for its retired Gurkha pensioners.

Alongside, till the mid-1990s, gallah-wallahs or recruiting sergeants from the Indian and British armies annually traversed eastern and western Nepal’s hilly regions, talent spotting Rai, Gurung, Limbu, Tamang and Magar Gurkhas for enlistment into their respective armies. But in recent years, only a fourth of the Gurkhas recruited annually in the Indian Army were from Nepal. So much so that in April 2016, when the Army commissioned its Sixth Battalion of the First Gurkha Rifles (6/1GR) at Sabathu, 64 km north of Chandigarh, it comprised locally domiciled Gurkhas and other recruits from the northeast.

Military analyst Lieutenant General H.S. Panag (retired) is of the view that Gurkha soldiers were not only fighting men for the Indian Army, but Delhi’s ambassadors to Nepal upon retirement and had ‘contributed immensely’ towards maintaining good relations between the neighbours. “China,” he declared on The Print in late 2022, “is waiting in the wings and India cannot afford to forsake this diplomatic leverage”.

However, long before the British began recruiting Gurkhas, Nepali soldiers had served in the army of Maharaja Ranjit Singh at Lahore in the early 19th century. They came to be known as Lahure — a term derived from Lahore, then the capital of the Sikh kingdom- and one that has lived on in Nepal as a colloquial description of men who leave home to serve in foreign armies.

Ranjit Singh had recognised the legendary fighting potential of the kukri-wielding Gurkhas, with their blood-curdling ‘Ayo Gorkhali’ (The Gurkhas are upon you) battle cry and their motto ' Kaphar hunnu bhanda marnu ramro ' — it was better to die than to live like a coward. The late Field Marshal Sam Manekshaw, who served with the 8 Gurkha Rifles after independence, added to this folklore by declaring that if a man said he was not afraid of dying, he was either a liar or a Gurkha.

In the meantime, a more disturbing aspect for India over the Agnipath/Agniveer spat with Nepal was a spate of media reports that China was considering recruiting Gurkhas into its People's Liberation Army (PLA). These concerns first surfaced prominently in April 2021, when local and overseas media reports revealed that Beijing had made an informal proposal to Nepal to establish a special relationship with its army, modelled on its arrangement with India.

This issue resurfaced in May 2023, after Nepal had suspended recruitment under Agnipath, but the claims were never substantiated and in May 2023, The Kathmandu Post too debunked these assertions. Nepal's Ambassador to China, Bishnu Pukar Shrestha, also denied that any such proposal had been received or discussed, while a senior foreign ministry official also dismissed the reports, but a haze still persist over this matter.

In conclusion, Shah's forthcoming Delhi visit offers India an opportunity to resolve the Gurkha recruitment impasse politically, rather than allow it to languish in bureaucratic limbo between military headquarters and foreign ministries. It also offers both sides a chance to repair strained bilateral ties and strengthen India's position in a neighbourhood where almost all its relationships have become increasingly toxic and tenuous.

“Delhi needs to spell out clearly how the revised Agnipath arrangement would apply to Nepali recruits,” said a two-star Army veteran from the Gurkhas. Kathmandu, for its part, must decide whether the new terms adequately address its objections and whether age-old military ties between the two sides can be restored, he added, declining to be named.

With the presentation of credentials, Mr. Dalela formally assumes his responsibilities as India’s Ambassador to Nepal.

title: Nepal Supreme Court clears regulated cannabis cultivation for medicinal and industrial use - MMJDaily
description: Nepal Supreme Court clears regulated cannabis cultivation for medicinal and industrial use  MMJDaily
publisher.title: MMJDaily
full_article:
Nepal's Supreme Court has authorized regulated cannabis cultivation for medicinal, scientific, agricultural, horticultural and industrial purposes, decades after the Himalayan nation banned the crop in 1973. The ruling, issued in May 2025, orders the government to make "necessary arrangements" for the "controlled cultivation and production of cannabis." The court also called for wider consultations on recreational use. Court documents were destroyed in a fire that September during protests that toppled the government, and the full text of the ruling was released only this week.

Saroj Adhikari, one of the petitioners in the case, told AFP: "We feel grateful to the Supreme Court for this verdict." Nepal revoked licences for cannabis dealers in 1973 under international pressure during a US-led campaign against drugs. Before the ban, Kathmandu attracted thousands of foreign backpackers who bought hashish from government-licensed shops.

Former health minister Birodh Khatiwada, who sponsored a related parliamentary motion in 2020, says: "The decision came after a long wait." Khatiwada argues that regulation could create jobs and generate income while curbing illegal trade. "Many developed nations have adopted legal cultivation, and we should not delay for it," he told AFP. "It will also help to curb illegal smuggling of marijuana, from which only a few people are benefiting."

Cannabis grows wild in Nepal and has traditionally been used in food, textiles and remedies. Currently, marijuana dealers face up to 10 years in prison, and police seize and destroy thousands of plants each year. Adhikari told AFP: "The law restricts smoking marijuana. But it's very common, so instead of restricting it, if it is regulated by law with strong enforcement mechanisms, it can generate revenue for the nation."

India Under-19 began their ACC Men’s U-19 Asia Cup 2026 campaign with a convincing 10-wicket win over Nepal Under-19 at the Al Amerat Cricket Ground on Friday (Nov 6). A strong bowling display led by Ishan Sood and an unbeaten half-century from Aaryavir Sehwag helped India register a comfortable victory. After winning the toss and choosing to bowl, India bowled Nepal out for 128 in 42.3 overs. The Indian openers then chased down the target in just 19.1 overs without losing a wicket.

Aaryavir Sehwag, son of former India opener Virender Sehwag, led the chase with an unbeaten 70 off 52 balls. Captain Lakshya Rajesh Raichandani also played a crucial role, scoring 53 not out off 63 deliveries. The duo shared an unbeaten opening stand to guide India home.

Aaryavir played the attacking role, hitting regular boundaries, while Raichandani held his end firmly to complete the chase.

Earlier, Ishan Sood led India’s bowling attack with an impressive spell of 3/18 in 10 overs, including four maiden overs. He removed Prashiddha Jaishi (1), Suryanshu Koirala (5) and Nischal Chhetri (0), reducing Nepal to 27/3.

Niraj Kumar Yadav (20) and Darsh Sonar tried to steady the innings, but India continued to pick up wickets. Sonar top-scored with 43 off 93 balls, while wicketkeeper-batter Aashish Luhar added 29 off 45 deliveries.

Some 1,451 people died and about 5,700 people, including more than 600 foreigners, are missing after the Nepal-Tibet floods in August. (EPA Images pic)

KUALA LUMPUR : Families of the 54 Malaysian victims of the Nepal-Tibet flood tragedy in August will receive a one-off payment of RM10,000 each through the national disaster management agency.

Human resources minister R Ramanan said the matter was decided by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim at today’s Cabinet meeting.

“He said an order of priority had been set out: first the spouse, second the parents, and third the children. ‘We will issue the list,’ he told reporters after visiting the Deepavali carnival at the National Stadium today.

A total of 1,451 people were killed and about 5,700 people, including more than 600 foreign nationals, are missing after a devastating flood and debris flow on Aug 26, triggered by a glacial ice and rock avalanche in the upper catchment area of Lhende Khola in Tibet.
